bull_bear.body:
- Producer of premium-quality teas, positioned in the top-quality segment, which the Company says lets it cater to the needs of its valued customers and benefit from higher realisations on quality teas
- Consistent improvisation of field practices for better output
- Own estates with factories (organised sector) and continued investment in factory machinery to upgrade equipment and enhance tea quality
- ISO 9001:2015 certified with cordial industrial relations; manpower of 2346 as at 31st March 2026 versus 2312 a year earlier
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Weather dependence — the crop is at the mercy of rainfall — MD&A Risks & Concerns: 'The tea Industry is largely dependent on vagaries of weather and weather plays a major role in determining the final output of produce. Both excess and scarcity of rainfall play havoc with the final output of produce.' Production is seasonal, carried out only March to December, so a single bad season cannot be made up.
- Labour intensity, wage inflation and stringent labour laws — MD&A: the industry is highly labour intensive and subject to stringent labour laws; cost of production is substantially higher than other tea-producing countries and than the Small Tea Grower sector because of high labour wage and social cost, and 'Any further increase in wage will substantially hit the bottom line.' The Company employed 2346 people as at 31st March 2026. Shortage of labour is separately named as a threat.
- Structural cost disadvantage versus the unorganised sector, whose share keeps rising — Small tea growers and bought-leaf factories now contribute more than 56% of India's tea production and their share is increasing year on year. Their cost of production is significantly lower because they do not provide the Plantation Labour Act social security benefits the organised sector must provide — a permanent cost gap the Company cannot close.
- Price realisation risk — cheap tea supply and a decade of near-flat auction prices — 'The increase in availability of cheap teas has a negative impact on prices of all category of teas.' The CAGR of auction price realisations has been a modest 3.81% over the past decade; the all-India auction average fell to Rs.190.25 in FY2025-26 from Rs.202.74 in FY2024-25, and North India realisation fell from Rs.224.55 to Rs.207.52. FY26 results were lower mainly on account of lower average realisation of teas.
- Input-cost inflation squeezing estate viability — MD&A Outlook: input costs 'encompassing energy, fertilizers, and other farm inputs, have experienced significant increases, thereby exerting pressure on the viability of tea estates' — rising costs against stagnant selling prices, which management says may render the upcoming year particularly difficult for the sector.
- Oversupply and subdued demand, expected to persist — Directors' Report: current market sentiment is in a downturn from oversupply and subdued demand both domestically and internationally, and 'This challenging environment for the tea industry is anticipated to persist into the upcoming year.' Indian production rose to 1382.74 million kgs in FY26 from 1294.54 million kgs, adding to the supply overhang.
- Export-market exposure — geopolitical disruption and competition from lower-cost origins — 'The demand for tea exports is currently subdued, primarily due to the geopolitical unrest in the Gulf region.' The Company also names stiff competition from Kenya, Sri Lanka and China on export pricing, and imports of tea into India from Nepal and Kenya, as threats to the industry.
- Single-commodity, single-activity concentration with climate change as a long-run overlay — The Company's entire business is plantation, manufacture and sale of black teas, with no other revenue stream disclosed, so every risk above hits the whole business at once. Climate change is explicitly listed among the threats to the industry. The Board has adopted and implemented a Risk Management Policy to mitigate these risks.
- Leverage and interest cost rising against loss-making operations — MD&A note on significant ratio changes states the interest coverage ratio moved on 'increase in interest expenses of the Company in the year under review', and the net profit margin change 'resulted due to increase in borrowings and losses suffered by the company in the year under review' — a structural balance-sheet strain flagged by management itself in the Risks/ratios discussion.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

The business is seasonal, with production carried out from March to December and subject to the vagaries of nature.

outlook.body:
- Stay positioned in the top-quality (premium) segment of black tea, on the view that the Company 'being in quality segment will gain from increase in average realisation of quality teas'.
- Consistently improvise field practices for better output.
- Sustain a replantation / rehabilitation programme on the estates — 20.36 hectares replanted, 12.22 hectares rehabilitated and 8.94 hectares uprooted in FY2025-26.
- Invest in factory machinery to upgrade the machineries and enhance the quality of teas.
- Maintain a steadfast commitment to producing high-quality tea as the route to navigating the current downturn.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body:
- Positive: India is the world's second largest tea consumer and per-capita consumption of tea in India is increasing every year; customers now prefer quality tea and are willing to pay more for it, so increasing consumer awareness for quality, branding and promotion will have a positive impact on domestic prices.
- Negative: the increase in availability of cheap teas has a negative impact on prices of all categories of tea; the unorganised sector (small tea growers and bought-leaf factories) is now more than 56% of country production and operates at a significantly lower cost because it does not provide the Plantation Labour Act social security benefits the organised sector provides.
- Outlook: the compounded annual growth rate of auction price realisations has been modest at 3.81% over the past decade while input costs — energy, fertilizers and other farm inputs — have risen significantly, pressuring the viability of tea estates.
- Export demand is currently subdued, primarily due to the geopolitical unrest in the Gulf region; there is also stiff competition from Kenya, Sri Lanka and China on export pricing and imports of tea from Nepal and Kenya.
- Domestic market prices are lower than the same period in the preceding year; rising costs against stagnant selling prices may render the upcoming year particularly difficult for the sector.
- Current market sentiment is in a downturn from oversupply and subdued demand both domestically and internationally, and this challenging environment is anticipated to persist into the upcoming year.
- North India April 2026 production rose to 85.34 million kg from 76.94 million kg in April 2025, but the Company's own tea production figures remain lower.
- FY26 results were lower mainly on account of lower average / price realisation of teas.
- Structural threats named: weather (both excess and scarcity of rainfall), climate change, high labour wage and social cost, and shortage of labour.

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Indian domestic tea market (auction and quality segment)
- Tea exports (described as currently subdued due to geopolitical unrest in the Gulf region)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Positive: India is the world's second largest tea consumer and per-capita consumption of tea in India is increasing every year; customers now prefer quality tea and are willing to pay more for it, so increasing consumer awareness for quality, branding and promotion will have a positive impact on domestic prices.
- Negative: the increase in availability of cheap teas has a negative impact on prices of all categories of tea; the unorganised sector (small tea growers and bought-leaf factories) is now more than 56% of country production and operates at a significantly lower cost because it does not provide the Plantation Labour Act social security benefits the organised sector provides.
- Outlook: the compounded annual growth rate of auction price realisations has been modest at 3.81% over the past decade while input costs — energy, fertilizers and other farm inputs — have risen significantly, pressuring the viability of tea estates.
- Export demand is currently subdued, primarily due to the geopolitical unrest in the Gulf region; there is also stiff competition from Kenya, Sri Lanka and China on export pricing and imports of tea from Nepal and Kenya.
- Domestic market prices are lower than the same period in the preceding year; rising costs against stagnant selling prices may render the upcoming year particularly difficult for the sector.
- Current market sentiment is in a downturn from oversupply and subdued demand both domestically and internationally, and this challenging environment is anticipated to persist into the upcoming year.
- North India April 2026 production rose to 85.34 million kg from 76.94 million kg in April 2025, but the Company's own tea production figures remain lower.
- FY26 results were lower mainly on account of lower average / price realisation of teas.
- Structural threats named: weather (both excess and scarcity of rainfall), climate change, high labour wage and social cost, and shortage of labour.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Stay positioned in the top-quality (premium) segment of black tea, on the view that the Company 'being in quality segment will gain from increase in average realisation of quality teas'.
- Consistently improvise field practices for better output.
- Sustain a replantation / rehabilitation programme on the estates — 20.36 hectares replanted, 12.22 hectares rehabilitated and 8.94 hectares uprooted in FY2025-26.
- Invest in factory machinery to upgrade the machineries and enhance the quality of teas.
- Maintain a steadfast commitment to producing high-quality tea as the route to navigating the current downturn.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Producer of premium-quality teas, positioned in the top-quality segment, which the Company says lets it cater to the needs of its valued customers and benefit from higher realisations on quality teas
- Consistent improvisation of field practices for better output
- Own estates with factories (organised sector) and continued investment in factory machinery to upgrade equipment and enhance tea quality
- ISO 9001:2015 certified with cordial industrial relations; manpower of 2346 as at 31st March 2026 versus 2312 a year earlier

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Weather dependence — the crop is at the mercy of rainfall — MD&A Risks & Concerns: 'The tea Industry is largely dependent on vagaries of weather and weather plays a major role in determining the final output of produce. Both excess and scarcity of rainfall play havoc with the final output of produce.' Production is seasonal, carried out only March to December, so a single bad season cannot be made up.
- Labour intensity, wage inflation and stringent labour laws — MD&A: the industry is highly labour intensive and subject to stringent labour laws; cost of production is substantially higher than other tea-producing countries and than the Small Tea Grower sector because of high labour wage and social cost, and 'Any further increase in wage will substantially hit the bottom line.' The Company employed 2346 people as at 31st March 2026. Shortage of labour is separately named as a threat.
- Structural cost disadvantage versus the unorganised sector, whose share keeps rising — Small tea growers and bought-leaf factories now contribute more than 56% of India's tea production and their share is increasing year on year. Their cost of production is significantly lower because they do not provide the Plantation Labour Act social security benefits the organised sector must provide — a permanent cost gap the Company cannot close.
- Price realisation risk — cheap tea supply and a decade of near-flat auction prices — 'The increase in availability of cheap teas has a negative impact on prices of all category of teas.' The CAGR of auction price realisations has been a modest 3.81% over the past decade; the all-India auction average fell to Rs.190.25 in FY2025-26 from Rs.202.74 in FY2024-25, and North India realisation fell from Rs.224.55 to Rs.207.52. FY26 results were lower mainly on account of lower average realisation of teas.
- Input-cost inflation squeezing estate viability — MD&A Outlook: input costs 'encompassing energy, fertilizers, and other farm inputs, have experienced significant increases, thereby exerting pressure on the viability of tea estates' — rising costs against stagnant selling prices, which management says may render the upcoming year particularly difficult for the sector.
- Oversupply and subdued demand, expected to persist — Directors' Report: current market sentiment is in a downturn from oversupply and subdued demand both domestically and internationally, and 'This challenging environment for the tea industry is anticipated to persist into the upcoming year.' Indian production rose to 1382.74 million kgs in FY26 from 1294.54 million kgs, adding to the supply overhang.
- Export-market exposure — geopolitical disruption and competition from lower-cost origins — 'The demand for tea exports is currently subdued, primarily due to the geopolitical unrest in the Gulf region.' The Company also names stiff competition from Kenya, Sri Lanka and China on export pricing, and imports of tea into India from Nepal and Kenya, as threats to the industry.
- Single-commodity, single-activity concentration with climate change as a long-run overlay — The Company's entire business is plantation, manufacture and sale of black teas, with no other revenue stream disclosed, so every risk above hits the whole business at once. Climate change is explicitly listed among the threats to the industry. The Board has adopted and implemented a Risk Management Policy to mitigate these risks.
- Leverage and interest cost rising against loss-making operations — MD&A note on significant ratio changes states the interest coverage ratio moved on 'increase in interest expenses of the Company in the year under review', and the net profit margin change 'resulted due to increase in borrowings and losses suffered by the company in the year under review' — a structural balance-sheet strain flagged by management itself in the Risks/ratios discussion.
